title: The Trouble with Computers: Usefulness, Usability and Productivity

commentary_subject.book_title: The Trouble with Computers: Usefulness, Usability and Productivity

main_argument: Despite massive investment in Information Technology (IT) in the U.S., there has been a nil return on investment in terms of productivity improvements. The book argues that this is due to a failure to adopt User Centred Design, Development and Deployment (UCDD), and proposes UCDD as the solution.
key_points: U.S. expenditure on IT is about 10% of GNP, with $4 trillion invested since 1960.
Econometric and psychological evidence suggests that for every dollar spent on IT, the U.S. economy has benefited by just $1, indicating a nil return on investment.
IT has not delivered revolutionary productivity improvements, often only enabling more of the same tasks to be done more frequently.
New technologies seldom result in better products or lower costs, and replacing well-established paper-based routines with expensive IT systems can lead to problems.
The initial, easy gains from automating repetitive information handling were quickly exhausted, leaving harder problems that require redesigning entire workflows.
Little benefit is gained from highly paid individuals spending more time on tasks previously done quicker by lower paid staff.
User Centred Design, Development and Deployment (UCDD) is proposed as the solution, focusing on building systems that meet user needs and are usable by end-users.
UCDD necessitates continuous, iterative testing and trialling with small numbers of typical users throughout the design process.
The principles of UCDD are generalizable beyond IT to other design problems, such as household goods and urban planning (e.g., path design, stereo button layout).
The book is considered a classic text in Human-Computer Interaction, with a message relevant to all designers.
strengths: The book provides a comprehensive demolition of arguments for IT productivity using robust econometric and psychological evidence.
It offers a constructive solution (UCDD) to the identified problems, supported by examples of successful IT products.
The analysis is not 'wholly depressing' and provides a clear path forward for designers.
The book's advice is broadly applicable to various design challenges, demonstrating its wider relevance.
recommendations: Designers everywhere should take the message of User Centred Design, Development and Deployment (UCDD) to heart.
